finding.claim: reset_password_loose() compares the reset token with loose equality (==). PHP type juggling lets an attacker reset any account's password without knowing the token. Sending boolean true (e.g. from a JSON body) matches any non-empty string token in PHP 8, and int 0 matches non-numeric tokens in PHP 7. Numeric-string collisions also work in every version: a stored token like "0e12345" equals the attacker string "0" or "0e999".
finding.source: Attacker-supplied $email and $token (reset request parameters, possibly JSON-decoded so $token can be bool or int), plus a victim email that has a pending reset row
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = ... at reset.php:5-6, which sets the victim's password

trace.note: $email, $token and $new enter reset_password_loose() from the caller
The stored token is fetched for the attacker-chosen email
$row['token'] == $token uses loose comparison, which is bypassable via type juggling and 0e magic-hash equality
The password hash is overwritten for that email, giving account takeover

finding.guards_checked: No strict comparison, hash_equals or type cast on this path. No token expiry, attempt limit or rate limit. No caller is in the repo, so how $token is typed is unknown. The remaining path is string-only, but the 0e collision still works there if tokens can be numeric-like strings. The safe variant reset_password() at line 12 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, so it is not affected. The queries use $db->quote(), so there is no SQL injection.

verdict.guard_found: none on this path (no strict compare, cast, expiry or rate limit); the safe variant reset_password() at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with a string cast, but it is not the function flagged
verdict.reason: The loose `==` at reset.php:4 is real and unguarded, and the lines at 2-6 match the trace, but nothing in the repo calls reset_password_loose, so I can't tell whether $token can arrive as bool/int (needed for the bypass) or only as a string (where only a rare "0e..." stored token collides).

finding.claim: Neither reset function invalidates the reset token after a successful reset, and neither checks token expiry. A token that is leaked, intercepted or stale stays valid indefinitely and can be replayed to change the password again. There is also no throttling, so tokens can be brute-forced online.
finding.source: Attacker who has any previously issued or leaked reset token for an email, or who can guess tokens without limit
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... at reset.php:15-16 (and 5-6 in the loose variant)

trace.note: The token row is selected by email only. No created-at or expiry column is checked.
Token validated with hash_equals; there is no attempt counter
Password updated, but no DELETE or UPDATE on the resets table follows, so the token stays reusable

finding.guards_checked: No expiry check, no one-time-use deletion and no rate limiting in this file. Caller-side controls such as rate limiting or token cleanup elsewhere cannot be ruled out because the repo contains only this file. hash_equals gives constant-time comparison but does not address replay or expiry.

verdict.guard_found: none (hash_equals at reset.php:14 only gives constant-time comparison; no expiry, no token deletion, no rate limiting in the file)
verdict.reason: reset.php:13-17 selects the token by email only, compares it at line 14, and updates the password at 15-16 and returns true with no expiry check and no DELETE or UPDATE on `resets`, so a token stays replayable. Throttling cannot be ruled out because the file has no callers, so that part of the claim is unverified. The loose variant at line 4 also uses `==`.
